summary: We love space and space exploration, so we thought an arcade-style space mission game would be a cool way to bring those interests to life. Over two days, we used Claude and Godot to build it, incorporating the attached resource data provided to us to shape the missions and gameplay.
details:
Mission Control: Space Mission Design Game

Mission Control is an arcade-style interactive game for the design and simulation of space missions. This game allows players to feel the difficulties associated with planning, construction, and execution of space missions based on the realities of life. In the game, players take on the part of a mission director starting in a mission control room, where a laptop interface provides access to mission selection, spacecraft design, launch vehicle choice, and mission resource management. There are four missions in the game that have increasing difficulty: Earth Observer, Lunar Orbiter, Mars Orbiter, and Jupiter Polar Orbiter.

The players build their spacecrafts out of 50 components with different properties, pros, cons, and references to real-life missions. Such aspects of the spacecraft as mass, propulsion, power generation, communication, thermal management, and radiation protection must be taken into account before the launch. After the launch, players can track the performance of their spacecraft via live telemetry, monitoring such parameters as altitude, velocity, acceleration, atmospheric heating, delta-v, power, and radiation. Players can review previous missions in order to understand the factors behind their success or failure.

Data and educational value: we used the provided data about the resources in order to create the spacecraft components, rocket configurations, and missions setup. The game also uses real-life space missions and aerospace engineering concepts in order to make complex topics more understandable through interactive gameplay. The game aims at stimulating interest in space exploration and making players familiar with engineering decisions made when planning interplanetary missions.

Technology and development: The game was created using the Godot Engine and GDScript programming language. The mission, rocket, and spacecraft components data was stored in JSON files. Claude was used as an AI-assisted development tool. The project was completed within two days and focused on creating a simulation, mission control, and gameplay.

Creativity and design: the development team was interested in space and space exploration and wanted to make it interactive. Instead of an educational presentation, the arcade-inspired pixel art style was used to make players feel like they are really working in the mission control center. The game includes physics-based simulations of spacecraft engineering, resource management, and missions.

During the development, such aspects were considered as scientific relevancy, gameplay balance, accessibility, technical feasibility, and time limitation of two days for development. The aim was to make a product that is entertaining and educational at the same time allowing players to learn about the difficulties of space exploration through their engineering decisions.

Eventually, Mission Control aims at making aerospace engineering more accessible and stimulating interest in science and technology behind humanity's space exploration.
